description: Hi! I'm Julie (Space Jules) from Norway – offshore steward, ocean lover and AI creator who makes films and music about the sea. I'm joining solo for the Earth Information Jukebox challenge with Ocean Pulse: a small web app that turns NASA's film of ocean currents and 47 years of Arctic sea ice data into sound, so you can hear the sea and hear the ice disappear. Skills: storytelling, video, sound and design, with AI as my coding partner. Here to learn, have fun and nerd out about space!
summary:
Ocean Pulse is an Earth jukebox that lets you hear NASA's Earth visualizations. It plays NASA's film "Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature" from the Earth Information Center collection and reads it frame by frame in the browser: the colours inside a listening ring become sound, live. Cold water sounds deep, warm water sounds high, and a line of bells sweeps from west (left ear) to east (right ear). You choose which sea to listen to, or drag the ring anywhere on the map. A second track, Arctic Pulse, plays 47 years of Arctic sea ice together with NASA GISTEMP temperatures, so you can hear the ice breathe through the seasons and the breath get shallower.

Earth science is mostly shown as pictures, which shuts out blind and low-vision people. Ocean Pulse is built for them first: everything works from the keyboard, a screen reader is told in full sentences what the picture shows, and stereo carries real information. It needs no installation, no account and no server: just a link.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ocean Pulse is a web page with two tracks, like records in a jukebox. Pick one, press Play, and the page turns what is on screen into sound in real time. Nothing is pre-recorded.

Track 1, Ocean Pulse: NASA's film of one year of sea surface currents (ECCO2 model, March 2007 to March 2008) plays on screen. You choose where to listen: the whole ocean, seven named regions (Gulf Stream, Equatorial Pacific, Indian Ocean, Kuroshio, Agulhas, Southern Ocean, Norwegian Sea), or any point you drag the ring to.

- Pitch of the low tone = sea surface temperature inside the ring (cold is deep, warm is high).

- Bells = a line sweeps the ring from west to east; each bell is the temperature of one slice, panned from the left ear to the right. A missing bell is land.

- Brightness and trembling = how dense and bright the current lines are and how much the picture moves.

Track 2, Arctic Pulse: 572 months of Arctic sea ice extent (January 1979 to October 2026).

- Pitch = ice extent (less ice sounds higher). Trembling and wind = Arctic air temperature that year. A low bell marks each March maximum and a higher bell each September minimum. A crack marks every new record-low September since 1990.

Both tracks follow one rule: a warmer world sounds higher.

HOW IT WORKS

Each video frame is drawn onto a hidden 360 x 180 canvas, so one analysed pixel is one degree of longitude by one degree of latitude. Grey pixels are land, coloured pixels are current lines, black pixels are water with no line. The hue of each line is converted back to a temperature using NASA's own colour bar (0 to 32 degrees C). Averages are weighted by the cosine of latitude, because a flat map stretches the poles. The numbers drive a small synthesizer built with the Web Audio API: a drone, a bell voice, filtered noise and a generated reverb. All notes are tuned to a five-note (pentatonic) scale, so any data pattern stays pleasant to listen to. That is how we balance strict data translation with musicality.

ACCESSIBILITY

- Full keyboard control: Space plays or pauses, arrow keys move the listening ring or step through time, D speaks a description.

- A live text region describes the scene in full sentences, for example: "Gulf Stream, 38 degrees north, 60 degrees west. June 2007. The sea surface here is about 21 degrees C. It is warmer to the south." It speaks only now and then, so speech does not drown the sound.

- The track list is a real radio group and sliders announce values in words.

- Large controls, visible focus, high contrast, and stereo used as information.

HONEST LIMITS

Temperatures in track 1 are estimates read from the colours of the picture, good to within a few degrees; they are not the original model output. The film shows one model year, not a trend. The ice cap drawn in track 2 is a stylised disc whose area is to scale; it is not a map.

BENEFITS AND HOPES

A blind student can explore where the ocean is warm and cold with their ears. A sighted listener notices things the eye skips, such as how sharply the temperature changes across the Gulf Stream, or how the September ice minimum drops step by step. We hope it can be used in classrooms, museums and at the Earth Information Center itself, and that more NASA visualizations can be added as new tracks: any film that comes with a colour bar can be read the same way.

TOOLS

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Canvas 2D for reading video pixels, Web Audio API for sound. No frameworks, no libraries, no server code, no tracking. Hosted on Netlify. Tested in Chromium on desktop and at phone width.


USE OF AI

The HTML, CSS and JavaScript were written with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic) during the hackathon, directed, tested and reviewed by the team. The README and this text were drafted with AI assistance and edited by the team. The idea is the team's own. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used: the picture is NASA's film, unchanged, and the sound is synthesised live from the data by ordinary oscillators and filters.

DATA AND CREDITS

Picture: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS 3912, ECCO2 model). Arctic air temperature: NASA GISS GISTEMP v4, zonal annual means 64N-90N. Sea ice: NSIDC Sea Ice Index, Version 4 (G02135). No third-party code libraries, fonts, images or sounds are used. NASA does not endorse this project.
